findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer plainly what Athena is and what sets it apart. This part works well.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The title and heading are about firstmate, a project the newcomer has probably never heard of, not about Athena. Someone arriving at the Athena site may think they are on the wrong page until they read the third paragraph.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title> and h1 of the same text

findings.text: The page says why the study exists, but it doesn't link the study to Athena's main job of turning a request into a change. A newcomer is left wondering whether the study shows off the product or is a side feature.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: An early link to next steps and a clear closing section mean the newcomer knows where to go. This works well.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" (header) and the "Next steps" section

findings.text: The install steps skip how to get a checkout, what tools or AI model access are needed, and what `athena ask` will produce or change. A newcomer can't safely try it from this page alone and has to go to the repository.
findings.source: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" / "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: Most of the page is a state machine of firstmate's internals, using terms like exit codes, pending-close records and stale wakes. This is far more detail than a newcomer wants, and the same facts appear several times across Start here, the transition cards and the Glossary.
findings.source: "Read each line as the state's name, its kind, and the claims that support it."; transition cards such as "t2 queued → queued" with "exit 75"

findings.text: The page says openly where its source is silent. That helps trust, but it is another layer of caveats a first-time reader has to work through.
findings.source: "in scope ... The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."

findings.text: The study admits its first pass missed whole paths and that nothing was run. That is honest, but a newcomer judging Athena may read it as a sign of weak reliability, and the page gives no context for it.
findings.source: "f3 ... A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths ... none was run, so no run confirmed that a script behaves as its header says."

findings.text: This section means nothing to a newcomer, who doesn't know what the `studies/` folder is or where it lives.
findings.source: "About this page: This page's study id, firstmate-work-handling, is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
